title: FAA Hires Over 2,000 Air Traffic Controllers After Targeting Gamers in Recruitment Push
excerpt: The unconventional campaign attracted 12,350 applications — more than double the previous record — as the agency works to close a shortage of 3,500 controllers.
body:
• The FAA hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers in 2026 and hit 94% of its recruitment goal after launching a campaign targeting video game players
  • The April campaign generated 12,350 applications, more than double the previous record, with 10,779 identified as qualified candidates
  • Research shows gamers excel at multitasking, spatial awareness, and attentional control — skills directly transferable to air traffic control
  • The FAA remains approximately 3,500 controllers short of its target staffing level of 14,600, a shortage linked to flight delays and safety concerns

The Federal Aviation Administration has hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers this year after an unconventional recruitment campaign that specifically targeted video game players — and the results have exceeded expectations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced that the agency has hit 94% of its recruitment goal, calling the effort "wildly successful" after the campaign generated 12,350 applications, more than double the previous record. Of those applicants, 10,779 were identified as qualified for air traffic controller roles.

From Gaming to Air Traffic Control

The FAA launched its gamer-focused ad campaign on April 10, urging players to "level up" and apply for positions starting April 17. A promotional video opened with Xbox branding and Twitch stream footage before cutting to a montage of air traffic controllers managing live airspace. "You've been training for this," the ad declared.

https://x.com/Newsforce/status/2086909398987800767

The pitch was grounded in research. The FAA cited studies showing that hardcore gamers demonstrate "high cognitive functions" including multitasking, spatial awareness, strategic thinking, and problem-solving — precisely the skills required to manage dozens of aircraft simultaneously across multiple radar screens.

"We're building the strongest, sharpest workforce in aviation history."

— Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation

A 2024 internal FAA poll found that only two out of 250 air traffic academy graduates were not gamers. Earlier academic research supported the connection: a 2006 study showed gamers were better at tracking multiple objects simultaneously, and a 2024 study confirmed those findings while also identifying superior "attentional control" among regular players.

Addressing a Critical Shortage

The hiring push comes as the FAA faces a persistent staffing crisis. The agency is approximately 3,500 controllers short of its target level of more than 14,600 and has 10% fewer controllers than it did in 2012. Just under 11,000 certified controllers are currently in service.

The shortage has had real consequences. Controllers at many facilities work mandatory overtime and six-day weeks. The understaffing has coincided with a troubling series of aviation incidents. In March 2026, an Air Canada flight crashed into a firetruck on the runway at LaGuardia Airport, killing the jet's two pilots. Investigators are examining whether an air traffic controller stepped away to answer an emergency phone call just before the collision.

In the January 2025 Reagan National Airport disaster, one controller had been doing the job of two people when an American Airlines regional jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter, killing all 67 people aboard the aircraft.

A Non-Traditional Pipeline

The gamer recruitment strategy reflects a broader shift in how the FAA identifies talent. Only about 25% of current controllers hold a traditional college degree, and the agency has increasingly focused on reaching candidates pursuing alternative career paths.

"This campaign's innovative communication style and focus on gaming taps into a growing demographic of young adults who have many of the hard skills it takes to be a successful controller," Duffy said.

The numbers support the approach. More than 200 million Americans regularly play video games, an industry that now generates more revenue than the film and music industries combined, according to PwC. With starting salaries reaching up to $155,000 and no college degree required, air traffic control offers a compelling career path for skilled gamers.

What's Next

The FAA has increased controller hiring every year since 2021. Transportation Secretary Duffy plans to ask Congress for tens of billions of dollars to upgrade aging FAA technology and facilities alongside the continued hiring push. The campaign's success suggests the gamer pipeline may become a permanent feature of the agency's recruitment strategy.

The newly hired controllers will undergo rigorous training at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City before being assigned to facilities nationwide. The full training process typically takes two to four years before a controller becomes fully certified.
